name: Buffy Brown
lede: Buffy Brown is a light tan-brown from Ridgway's 1912 nomenclature that turns out to be one of the most common colors in the whole ColorHub painting archive.

sections.title: A buff tone, systematized
sections.body:
Ridgway's *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* (1912) lists Buffy Brown on plate XL, hue 17′′′, tone i, built on *buff*, the pale tan of undyed leather [1]. The ISCC-NBS system placed it in its 1955 block 76, *light yellowish brown* [1]. In printed English the phrase itself rose fastest in the 1900s and peaked in the 1940s, though that count mixes the color sense with the unrelated adjective *buffy* [1].

The library's measurements place its nearest named neighbor as [[folkstone|Folkstone]], 2.7 units off, with [[broccoli-brown|Broccoli Brown]] close behind at 3.5, and it sits about 6.9 units from the everyday name [[taupe|Taupe]] [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a color match to this swatch in 4,639 of 23,781 paintings, 19.51 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 2,882, more common than 98 percent of the named colors we track [3]. George Catlin is its most devoted painter, carrying it in 21 of the 50 [[painter:george-catlin|Catlin]] paintings in the archive, 3.6 times the rate expected from the museums his works come from, with Martinus Rørbye, Kano Tan'yū and George Hendrik Breitner all well above average [3].

The color's deepest historical cluster is the 1100s, when it fills half of the 50 paintings we have from then, and inside a painting it most often plays a light tone (35 percent of its 2,882 within-painting matches) [3]. The earliest match dates to the year 900, more than a thousand years before the name's 1912 record, which shows only that a similar-looking hue existed in paint long before the word did, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. It shares canvases with Olive-Brown and Long Beach far more than chance [3]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, read as screen colors [3].
